name: The Bacchic/Orphic religious current and its influence on philosophy
plain_explanation: Alongside the calm, human-like Olympian gods of Homer, many Greeks worshipped Dionysus (Bacchus), a god of wine and ecstatic intoxication imported from Thrace. Out of this cult grew Orphism, a more disciplined, ascetic reform movement that taught the transmigration of souls and the possibility of purifying the soul to escape an endless cycle of birth and death.
precise_definition: A tradition running from the primitive, ecstatic worship of Dionysus to its Orphic reform, which substituted mental for physical intoxication ('enthusiasm', having the god enter the worshipper), taught the soul's immortality and transmigration, held the body to be 'the tomb of the soul', and pursued purification through ascetic rules and ritual.
why_it_mattered: Russell argues this mystical current, not the sober Olympian religion, is the direct ancestor of the specifically religious and otherworldly strand in Greek philosophy, entering it through Pythagoras and, from him, through Plato into much of later philosophy and Christian theology.
historical_origin: Dionysus was originally a Thracian fertility god; his cult migrated to Greece shortly before historical times and was reformed, in the more mystical and ascetic direction, into Orphism, traditionally associated with the figure of Orpheus.
associated_philosopher: Pythagoras (as the philosopher through whom Orphic elements entered Greek philosophy)
examples: Orphic tablets found in tombs instructing the soul how to find the Well-spring of Memory in the afterlife
The Bacchae of Euripides, dramatizing both the beauty and savagery of Dionysiac ritual
Pythagorean and Orphic rules of abstinence and purification
competing_positions: The rationalist, empirical, Olympian-religious tendency represented by Homer, Herodotus, and the early Ionian philosophers
influence_on_later_thinkers: Passed via Pythagoras into Plato's doctrine of the soul and the intelligible world, and from Plato into later religious and Christian philosophy.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious in origin; Orphic communities were also unusual in admitting members without regard to race or sex, giving rise, Russell suggests, to philosophy conceived as a whole way of life.
